---
title: |
  Whose Polarization? Party Attachment and the Many Faces of Polarization in 25 European Democracies
abstract: |
  Polarization describes how orientations are distributed in a population, and research on affective polarization usually takes that population to be partisans.
  Who counts as a partisan, however, is rarely argued.
  Studies define the in-party by a reported attachment or by the vote, as if the two were interchangeable, while the share of citizens who report an attachment differs widely across European democracies.
  I argue that this choice is itself a claim about what partisanship is.
  If attachment merely restates the vote, conditioning on it is harmless; if it is an identity, the polarization of partisans is a different phenomenon from the polarization of voters.
  European multiparty systems allow this to be examined, because attachment and vote come apart.
  I compare voters of the same party who report an attachment with voters who deny one, across six facets of polarization: ideological extremity and sorting, perceived party polarization and sorting, affect toward parties, and behavior toward other citizens in trust and dictator games with randomized partner parties.
  Combining the European Election Studies, the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems, the European Social Survey and a 2019 survey of 25 democracies, the design traces the partisan composition of European electorates in the 21st century, the profile of attachment's contribution across facets, its variation across countries, and how much change in polarization reflects change in who is partisan.

This draft sets out the argument and the research design.
The empirical sections (@sec-composition to @sec-decomposition) are placeholders that state what each analysis will show and how it will be read.
No estimates are reported, and no finding is claimed.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Every claim about polarization is a claim about a distribution.
To say that a society is polarized is to say that some orientation, be it a policy position, a perception of the parties, a feeling toward them or a way of treating other citizens, is spread out, clustered at opposing ends, or aligned with other orientations among some set of people.
The concept therefore leaves a question open that is easily passed over: whose orientations are we describing?
The answer fixes the population of inference, and with it what any estimate of polarization can mean.

Research answers this question in different ways, and often without saying so.
The distinction between elites and the mass public is well established, and I set it aside here to focus on the mass public.
Within the mass public, however, the population varies from study to study.
Measures of affective polarization (AP) are computed among partisans only [@reiljan2020fear], across the whole electorate [@wagner2021affective], or with the in-party defined by the vote [@harteveld2021fragmentedfoes].
In the United States, part of the dispute over whether the public has polarized or merely sorted turned on whether one looks at party identifiers or at the public at large [@fiorina2008polarization].
Partisans themselves are defined in some studies by a reported attachment and in others by the vote, as if the two were interchangeable.

In comparative research, this choice has consequences.
An index computed among partisans mixes two quantities: who the partisans are, and how polarized they are.
The share of citizens who report an attachment differs across countries, across question wordings and across years (@sec-composition).
Comparisons of partisan-only measures across countries or over time therefore confound the composition of the partisan population with the polarization within it, and partisan-only and electorate-wide measures can indeed trace different trends [@garzia2023affective].

The problem is not merely one of choosing the right denominator.
Restricting the population to those who report an attachment, rather than to those who vote for a party, is harmless only if the attachment adds nothing beyond the vote.
If attachment merely restates a vote choice, the two populations describe the same phenomenon.
If attachment is a group identity, the polarization of partisans is a different phenomenon from the polarization of voters, and the choice of population decides which one is measured.
The measurement choice thus presupposes an answer to a substantive question: what does party attachment itself contribute to polarization?

Two literatures each answer half of this question.
European electoral research asked early on whether party identification is distinct from the vote in multiparty systems at all [@budge1976party; @shively1979development; @thomassen2005theeuropean], and whether attachment should be understood as an affective tie or as an evaluation [@holmberg2007partisanship].
That debate concerned vote choice, not polarization.
Research on AP, in turn, asks whether citizens dislike their opponents because of a group identity or because of the policies that identity signals [@dias2022nature; @orr2023affective; @webster2017ideological; @lelkes2021policy].
That debate is conducted mainly in a two-party system where attachment, vote and policy package coincide, so that even experimental manipulations of partisan identity shift perceived policy agreement [@orr2023affective].
Neither literature estimates the contribution of attachment with the vote held fixed, and neither does so across the different facets of polarization.

European multiparty systems allow both.
Because attachment and vote come apart, voters of the same party differ in whether they report an attachment to it.
Comparing them within the party holds fixed the party's policy signal, the set of out-parties its voters face, and the cues its elites send.
Every respondent also faces several out-parties at different policy distances, which allows distance to vary within a person.
A cross-national survey of 25 European democracies fielded in 2019 adds trust and dictator games in which the partner's party is randomized [@hahm2024divided].
I classify respondents into partisan types by crossing attachment with the vote, and I compare them on six facets of polarization, using the European Election Studies (EES), the Comparative Study of Electoral Systems (CSES), the European Social Survey (ESS) and the 2019 survey (EU25).

The paper asks four research questions (RQs):

- **RQ1 (who).** How common is each partisan type across European electorates, and has the partisan composition changed since 2000?
- **RQ2 (whether and what kind).** Does attachment add to polarization beyond the vote, on which facets, and through attachment to the in-group or rejection of the out-group?
- **RQ3 (where).** Does the contribution of attachment vary across countries and parties?
- **RQ4 (so what).** Do changes in who is partisan, or changes in how polarized partisans are, account for changes in polarization?

The paper contributes to three literatures.
For research on polarization and its measurement, it makes the choice of population explicit and shows how much it matters for comparisons across countries and over time (RQ1, RQ4).
For research on partisanship, it answers the long-standing European question of what an attachment is by examining its consequences rather than its correlates (RQ2).
For comparative research, it provides a 21st-century account of partisan composition in 25 democracies and a decomposition of polarization change into composition and change within partisan types (RQ1, RQ3, RQ4).

@sec-concepts defines the facets of polarization, the partisan types and three readings of what partisanship is.
@sec-expectations derives what each reading implies for each facet.
@sec-design sets out the research design.
@sec-composition to @sec-decomposition hold the analyses, one per RQ, and @sec-limitations collects the limitations.
One caveat applies throughout: the within-party comparison brackets the contribution of attachment rather than identifying it, and the only quantity with a causal interpretation is the effect of the partner's party label in the games.

# Polarization and Partisanship {#sec-concepts}

## Polarization as a Distribution {#sec-polarization}

I distinguish the facets of polarization along two dimensions.
The first is the *object* of the orientation: a citizen's own policy positions, their perceptions of where the parties stand, their feelings toward the parties, and their behavior toward other citizens.
The second is the *form* of polarization: its *level*, meaning how extreme or how far apart orientations are, or its *structure*, meaning how strongly orientations on different dimensions are aligned.
Applied to the left–right (LR) and European integration (EU) dimensions, this yields six facets, which I always discuss in the same order: (1) ideological extremity, (2) ideological sorting, (3) perceived party polarization, (4) perceived party sorting, (5) vertical attitudinal AP, that is, feelings toward parties, and (6) horizontal behavioral AP, that is, behavior toward citizens who support a party.
Ratings of party supporters in the EES 2024 provide horizontal attitudinal AP as a complement.

Studying all six facets together is necessary for the question at hand.
The accounts of partisanship discussed below agree that partisans dislike opposing parties more than other citizens do.
They disagree about *where* the attachment acts: on the positions citizens hold, on how they see the parties, or on how they feel about and treat their opponents.
A study of one facet cannot tell the accounts apart.
Only the pattern of the attachment's contribution across facets can.

## Attachment and Vote {#sec-types}

Party attachment is a standing tie that a citizen reports when asked whether they feel close to a party.
The vote is a single act at one election.
Crossing the two, and adding the leaner probe where a survey fields one, yields five partisan types (@tbl-types).

| Reports an attachment | Leans when probed | Reports a vote | Partisan type |
|---|---|---|---|
| yes | — | yes, for the same party | explicit partisan |
| no | no (or not asked) | yes | denier |
| no | yes, toward the party voted for | yes | leaner |
| yes | — | yes, for a different party | mismatched partisan |
| no | no (or not asked) | no | non-partisan |

: Partisan types from the attachment × vote tree {#tbl-types}

The central type is the denier: a vote-anchored respondent who reports voting for a party but answers that they feel close to none.
Deniers are the empirical form of the conceptual distinction between attachment and vote, since they share the act with explicit partisans of their party but not the tie.
The other types extend the comparison.
Leaners, available only where a probe was fielded, allow the attachment to be graded rather than treated as present or absent.
Mismatched partisans separate attachment from vote, since they share the attachment with the explicit partisans of one party and the vote with the deniers of another.
Non-partisans, who report neither, provide the baseline against which the other types are compared.

## Three Readings of Partisanship {#sec-readings}

What, then, could an attachment add to a vote?
The literature offers three readings.

The **functional reading** holds that in multiparty systems a reported attachment largely restates the vote.
In this view, rooted in Shively's functional model of party identification [@shively1979development], expressed partisanship becomes "synonymous with the vote" where parties do not serve as independent guides to behavior [@thomassen2005theeuropean, ch. 1].
Comparative work found that partisanship and the vote have become more independent over time [@thomassen2005theeuropean, ch. 5], and in the Netherlands, party identification has been treated as partly endogenous to the vote [@van2021dealignment].
If this reading holds, explicit partisans and deniers of the same party should not differ on any facet.

The **evaluative reading** holds that an attachment is a standing judgment of a party's policies and performance, a running tally of past evaluations [@fiorina1981retrospective].
Holmberg argues that the Michigan concept has been stretched to cover both an affective attachment and such an evaluative partisanship, and that the two should be measured separately [@holmberg2007partisanship].
Richardson describes European partisanship in the 1980s as "cognitive partisanship to a substantial degree" [@richardson1991european], and work outside Europe describes partisanship as a standing choice that tracks performance [@mattes2020theconsequences].
If this reading holds, the attachment adds most where policy is: in the positions citizens hold and in the policy content of their judgments of parties.

The **identity reading** holds that an attachment is a group identity [@campbell1960american; @green2004partisan].
Identity-based measures predict party ratings and political activity beyond the conventional strength item [@greene2004social; @bankert2017measuring].
Huddy, Bankert and Davies find the expressive pattern among strong partisans in four European countries and conclude that Europe and the United States differ in the level of partisanship, not its nature [@huddy2018expressive].
Stable partisans of cleavage parties in Britain and the Netherlands were found to hold hostile views of other cleavage parties [@richardson1991european].
If this reading holds, the attachment adds little to positions and most to how citizens see, feel about and treat their opponents.

The identity reading has two variants, because an identity can operate through attachment to the in-group or through rejection of out-groups.
Research on negative partisanship shows that rejection of a party is distinct from attachment to another and has its own consequences [@rose1998negative; @medeiros2014forgotten; @mayer2017how; @samuels2018partisans].
Hostility toward opponents tracks negative partisan identity more closely than positive identity [@bankert2023politics], and in France, ties to parties increasingly rest on rejection [@tiberj2025parties].
The **in-group variant** locates the attachment's contribution in warmth toward one's own party and favoritism toward its supporters.
The **out-group variant** locates it in dislike of opposing parties and derogation of their supporters.

## Measurement as a Conceptual Question {#sec-measurement}

How attachment is asked about is part of what it means.
Survey items ask whether respondents feel *close* to a party far more often than whether they *identify* with one, and closeness may capture a tie to a party seen as a distinct object rather than a party that is part of oneself [@elliott2024like].
Closeness-only wordings can exclude weakly attached voters [@sinnott1998party], whereas leaners resemble weak partisans in how they vote and evaluate [@petrocik2009measuring].
Many citizens hold attachments to more than one party [@block2026partisan].
These points motivate the leaner and mismatched types.
They also make variation in wording across surveys both a resource, because a pattern that recurs across wordings is less likely to reflect one item, and a threat, because the same type may not mean the same thing in every survey (@sec-limitations).

## Dealignment as an Open Question {#sec-dealignment}

The composition of the partisan population is not fixed either.
The dominant account of the post-war period is one of partisan dealignment [@dalton2002parties], driven by political events [@crewe1977partisan] or by cognitive mobilization [@dalton1984cognitive].
Yet even for that period the decline was uneven: steep in some countries, cyclical in others and absent in yet others [@schmitt1998political], and not monotonic [@thomassen2005theeuropean].
Whether dealignment continued into the 21st century is an open question.
It has been asked whether German dealignment has halted [@arzheimer2017another], French closeness has declined since 2002 [@tiberj2025parties], and party systems whose parties take inconsistent positions have fewer partisans [@dassonneville2023partisan].
I therefore do not assume a trend.
Three trajectories are possible: continued dealignment, stabilization, or realignment, in which attachment shifts toward parties of a new cultural or transnational cleavage rather than disappearing [@kriesi2008west; @hooghe2018cleavage].
Which of them holds, and where, is the first empirical question of this paper (RQ1).

## The Party-versus-Policy Debate as a Special Case {#sec-special-case}

The American debate over whether partisans dislike each other because of party or because of policy [@dias2022nature; @orr2023affective] maps onto the contrast between the identity and the evaluative reading, applied to one facet in a system where the two are hard to separate.
This paper extends that debate in three ways.
It examines the other facets, which the two readings predict differently.
It holds the party's policy signal fixed by comparing voters of the same party.
And it distinguishes the in-group from the out-group variant of the identity reading.

# Expectations {#sec-expectations}

## The Logic of a Profile {#sec-profile-logic}

The quantity of interest is the gap between explicit partisans and deniers of the same party, written $\Delta$ and estimated separately for each facet.
The functional reading predicts that $\Delta$ is zero on every facet.
It is a null that the paper can lose to, and the design has to be able to show it.
The evaluative and identity readings both predict that $\Delta$ differs from zero, but they predict different *patterns* across facets.
The evidence is therefore the profile of $\Delta$, not any single estimate.

## The Ladder of Facets {#sec-ladder}

The order of the facets runs from a citizen's own positions, through perceptions of the parties and feelings toward them, to behavior toward other citizens.
Along this ladder, the orientations move from those that policy can explain to those that are increasingly about groups.
The evaluative reading therefore predicts that $\Delta$ is largest at the bottom of the ladder and fades toward the top.
The identity reading predicts the reverse: a small $\Delta$ on positions that grows through perceptions to affect and behavior.
The functional reading predicts a flat profile at zero.
The ladder also orders the threats to inference, which ease from reverse causation for positions, through sophistication for perceptions and selection through the vote for affect, to a randomized treatment in the games.

## Expectations by Facet {#sec-facet-expectations}

**Ideological extremity.** Under the evaluative reading, explicit partisans hold more extreme positions than deniers of the same party, because attachment forms around positions that set a party apart.
Under the identity reading, the gap in extremity is small, but explicit partisans cluster more tightly around their party's position, because identifiers follow their party's cues [@slothuus2021political; @bisgaard2018partisan].
The quantity that discriminates is the dispersion of positions within the party, not their level.
A larger extremity together with lower dispersion would mean that the facet cannot separate the readings on its own.

**Ideological sorting.** Under the evaluative reading, LR and EU positions are more strongly associated among explicit partisans within the same party, because coherent citizens are the ones who attach.
Under the identity reading, adopting the party's bundle compresses the variation among co-partisans and weakens the association within the party, while strengthening it between parties.
Both readings expect stronger sorting overall, so the quantity that discriminates is the sign of the gap within the party.
Because variation within a party is restricted, this facet has the least power.

**Perceived party polarization.** Under the evaluative reading, explicit partisans perceive the parties as further apart because they are better informed, so their placements track the parties' actual positions.
Under the identity reading, explicit partisans perceive the parties as further apart than they are, and the excess is concentrated in their placements of out-parties.
The quantity that discriminates is the excess of perceived over actual spread.
The evidence for false polarization comes mainly from the United States [@levendusky2016mis], so this expectation is the least grounded in European work and is treated as exploratory.

**Perceived party sorting.** Under the evaluative reading, explicit partisans perceive the parties' LR and EU positions as aligned to the extent that they actually are.
Under the identity reading, an us-versus-them lens lumps the out-parties together on both dimensions, so perceived alignment exceeds actual alignment, driven by the placements of out-parties.
The quantity that discriminates is the excess of perceived over actual alignment.

**Vertical attitudinal AP.** Both readings predict that dislike of a party rises with its policy distance from the respondent, as found in multiparty systems [@harteveld2021fragmentedfoes; @gidron2022dislikes].
They differ in what the attachment adds to this gradient.
Under the evaluative reading, attachment steepens the gradient, so the gap between explicit partisans and deniers disappears once distance to the rated party is held fixed.
Under the identity reading, attachment shifts the gradient, so the gap persists at equal distance.
The in-group variant locates the gap in ratings of one's own party, the out-group variant in ratings of the others.
For mismatched partisans, the identity reading predicts that the party they are attached to is rated at least as highly as the party they voted for, while the evaluative reading predicts the reverse.

**Horizontal behavioral AP.** In the games, the partner's party label shifts how many tokens respondents send, and the party label produces the largest penalty among the profile attributes [@hahm2024divided].
The identity reading predicts a larger label effect for explicit partisans than for deniers.
Its in-group variant locates the gap in favoritism toward co-partisans, relative to a partner whose party is not shown, and its out-group variant in derogation of out-partisans.
The evaluative reading predicts that derogation rises with the partner party's distance and that the gap between types is small.
Because the same respondents rate the parties, the identity reading also predicts a behavioral gap comparable to the attitudinal one, whereas the evaluative reading predicts a smaller behavioral gap.

@tbl-predictions summarizes the expectations.

| Facet | Functional reading | Evaluative reading | Identity reading | Discriminating quantity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ideological extremity | no gap | explicit partisans more extreme | little extra extremity; lower dispersion within the party | dispersion within the party |
| Ideological sorting | no gap | stronger association within the party | weaker within the party, stronger between parties | sign of the gap within the party |
| Perceived party polarization | no gap | larger spread that tracks actual positions | spread beyond actual positions, in out-party placements | excess over actual spread |
| Perceived party sorting | no gap | tracks actual alignment | out-parties lumped together; excess alignment | excess over actual alignment |
| Vertical attitudinal AP | no gap; mismatched rate the vote party higher | gap vanishes at equal distance; mismatched rate the vote party higher | gap persists at equal distance (in-group variant: in-party ratings; out-group variant: out-party ratings); mismatched rate the attachment party at least as high | gap at equal distance; locus; mismatched ratings |
| Horizontal behavioral AP | no gap | derogation rises with partner distance; small gap | larger label effect (in-group variant: favoritism; out-group variant: derogation); behavioral gap comparable to attitudinal | favoritism vs. derogation by type; distance gradient |

: Expectations of the three readings by facet, for the gap between explicit partisans and deniers of the same party {#tbl-predictions}

## Leaners and Mismatched Partisans {#sec-other-types}

The other types sharpen the test.
The functional reading implies that explicit partisans, leaners and deniers of the same party do not differ.
If attachment is graded, as both the evaluative and the identity reading allow, leaners should fall between explicit partisans and deniers.
Mismatched partisans provide the comparison with the fewest confounders in the design: their rating of the party they are attached to against the party they voted for is a comparison within one person, holding everything about that person fixed.

## Context {#sec-context-expectations}

The contribution of attachment need not be the same everywhere (RQ3).
Out-party hostility was strongest among supporters of old cleavage parties [@richardson1991european], which suggests larger gaps for cleavage parties.
The polarization of a party system has competing implications: it has been linked to stronger identification [@thomassen2005theeuropean, ch. 7], yet it also weakens the extent to which closeness to a party prevents switching [@dejaeghere2017comparative].
Attachments to parties of the new cultural cleavage may carry larger gaps, because identities have formed around that cleavage [@bornschier2021us; @zollinger2024cleavage].
Given 25 countries and noisy measures of context, I treat these as expectations that guide interpretation, not as hypotheses to be tested.

## Composition and Change {#sec-change-expectations}

Each trajectory of composition (@sec-dealignment) has its own implication for RQ4.
Under continued dealignment with *concentration*, the citizens who give up an attachment are the less engaged, as found for Germany [@dassonneville2012age], so the share of explicit partisans falls while $\Delta$ rises, and aggregate polarization can remain stable.
Under continued dealignment with *alienation*, citizens who give up an attachment become negative toward the party system [@dassonneville2018indifference], so negative affect appears among deniers and non-partisans who have no in-party.
Under stabilization, changes in polarization come from within partisan types.
Under realignment, new attachments to parties of the new cleavage carry a larger $\Delta$.

# Research Design {#sec-design}

The design rests on five elements: a comparison within the vote party, a set of partisan types that brackets the contribution of attachment, a randomized treatment that anchors one part of the inference, triangulation across sources, and a single estimation framework that delivers the European, comparative and dynamic quantities together.

## The Within-Party Contrast {#sec-contrast}

All comparisons are made among voters of the same party in the same country.
This holds fixed everything that is shared within a party and country: the platform and the policy signal it sends, the set of out-parties its voters face, the cues its elites send, and the national norms about admitting an attachment.
It rules out the explanation that explicit partisans differ from deniers only because they vote for different parties.
What the contrast does not hold fixed are individual characteristics that shape both attachment and polarization, such as socialization, political interest and ideological intensity.
Conditioning on the vote can also select respondents on the outcome: deniers may vote for a party partly because they dislike the alternatives.
And reported attachment and vote carry measurement error.

## Bracketing with Partisan Types {#sec-bracketing}

No single contrast identifies the contribution of attachment, because each is selected by the vote in its own way.
I therefore read the contrasts together.
The contrast between explicit partisans and deniers is a lower bound if deniers vote for their party partly out of dislike for the alternatives, and an upper bound if deniers are less engaged voters who vote out of habit.
The contrast between explicit partisans and non-partisans is likely an upper bound, because not voting and not attaching both tend to go with low engagement, so the contrast adds the vote and engagement to the attachment.
Mismatched partisans separate attachment from vote, and the comparison of non-partisans with deniers on characteristics that precede the vote shows whether the vote selects deniers on the outcome.
If the contrasts fall in the order their conditions imply, the contribution of attachment lies between them.
If they cross, at least one condition fails, and the diagnostics show which.

## A Randomized Anchor {#sec-anchor}

In the EU25 games, the partner's party is randomized within each partisan type.
The effect of the party label, $AP_t$, is therefore causal for each type.
The difference in this effect between explicit partisans and deniers, $\Delta$, is not, because the types themselves are not randomized.
Because the same respondents also rate the parties on thermometers, the comparison between attitudinal and behavioral AP is made within persons.

## Sources and Triangulation {#sec-sources}

Each source contributes a different part of the inference (@tbl-coverage).
The EES covers the period since 2004 with LR and EU self-placements, placements of the parties and propensity-to-vote (PTV) ratings, and in 2024 ratings of party supporters.
The CSES covers the period since 1996 with LR placements, like–dislike ratings of parties and a leaner probe in every module.
The ESS covers 2002 to 2024 with an attachment item and self-placements, which makes it the main source for composition.
The EU25 survey adds party thermometers and the games for one year, 2019.
Party attachments and votes are coded to Party Facts identifiers in all four sources and matched by one common rule.
Where the same pattern appears across sources that word the attachment item differently, it is unlikely to stem from one item.
Triangulation addresses measurement, however, and not confounding that all sources share.

| Facet | EES | CSES | ESS | EU25 (2019) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ideological extremity (self-placement) | LR, EU | LR (EU only in some studies) | LR; EU (some rounds) | LR, EU |
| Ideological sorting (LR × EU self-placement) | where both asked | rarely | some rounds | yes |
| Perceived party polarization (party placements) | LR, EU | LR | — | LR, EU |
| Perceived party sorting (LR × EU party placements) | where both asked | — | — | yes |
| Vertical attitudinal AP (party ratings) | PTV (all waves) | like–dislike of parties and leaders | — | thermometer (six parties) |
| Horizontal AP (toward partisans) | like–dislike of party supporters (2024; attitudinal) | — | — | dictator and trust games (behavioral) |

: Facets of polarization by data source {#tbl-coverage}

## Estimation Strategy {#sec-estimation}

The quantities of interest are contrasts of marginal means.
For a facet with outcome $Y$, the gap between explicit partisans and deniers is

$$
\Delta = \sum_{p} w_p \left[ E(Y \mid \text{explicit}, p) - E(Y \mid \text{denier}, p) \right],
$$

where $p$ indexes the vote parties in which both types occur and $w_p$ are common party weights.
For AP, the type-specific gap between ratings of co-partisan and out-partisan targets is $AP_t = E(Y \mid \text{co}, t) - E(Y \mid \text{out}, t)$.
In the games it is split into in-group favoritism, $E(Y \mid \text{co}, t) - E(Y \mid \text{control}, t)$, and out-group derogation, $E(Y \mid \text{control}, t) - E(Y \mid \text{out}, t)$, where the control is a co-national partner whose party is not shown.
Quantities that describe a group, such as dispersion or alignment, are computed on each type's predicted distribution under the same party weights, so that a difference between types cannot reflect a difference in the parties they vote for.
All estimates are expressed in standard-deviation units so that facets can be compared.

The estimates come from Bayesian multilevel models in which respondents are nested in parties, countries and surveys, with time entering as a trend.
Partial pooling yields, from one framework, the pooled European contrast, its variation across countries and its change over time.
The decomposition of change into the mix of types and change within types is computed on the posterior draws.
The models are built up step by step, and the same estimand is computed at every step, so that a change in the estimate shows which part of the model drives it.

## Reading Rules {#sec-reading-rules}

Four rules for interpretation are fixed before the results.
First, because conditioning on the vote plausibly pulls the AP gap toward zero, a positive gap is conservative and a null is weak evidence.
Second, gaps in ideology are read as associations net of party sorting, because ideology may cause attachment.
Third, the perception facets are exploratory, because sophistication may make explicit partisans more accurate rather than more biased.
Fourth, variation across countries is described, not explained.
@sec-limitations states the limits of each facet in full.

# Who Is Partisan? {#sec-composition}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** RQ1: the shares of explicit partisans, deniers, leaners, mismatched partisans and non-partisans by country and year, since 2000.
- **Expectation.** Continued dealignment, stabilization or realignment (@sec-dealignment), by country.
- **Exhibit.** Type shares by country × period, with the effects of study and wording modelled; the shift of attachment across party families as the test of realignment.
- **Reading.** Which trajectory holds where, and how large the problem of comparing partisan-only measures (@sec-intro) is in practice.
- **Limits.** Trends partly reflect switches between studies and wordings; a denier in the ESS is not the same category as a probed denier in the CSES (@sec-limitations).
:::

# What Attachment Adds {#sec-contribution}

Each analysis follows the same template: the question, the expectations from @sec-facet-expectations, the estimate of $\Delta$, its reading against the three readings, and its limits.

## Ideological Extremity {#sec-res-extremity}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** Within the same party, do explicit partisans hold more extreme LR and EU positions than deniers, and are their positions less dispersed?
- **Expectation.** @tbl-predictions, row 1: dispersion within the party discriminates.
- **Exhibit.** $\Delta$ in extremity and in dispersion; $\Delta$ by party position.
- **Limits.** Reverse causation; selection on proximity (@sec-limitations).
:::

## Ideological Sorting {#sec-res-sorting}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** Are LR and EU positions more or less strongly associated among explicit partisans than among deniers of the same party, within and between parties?
- **Expectation.** @tbl-predictions, row 2: the sign of the gap within the party discriminates.
- **Exhibit.** $\Delta$ in the strength of the LR–EU association within and between parties.
- **Limits.** Restricted range within parties; coverage; low power (@sec-limitations).
:::

## Perceived Party Polarization {#sec-res-perceived-polarization}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** Do explicit partisans perceive the parties as further apart than deniers of the same party, and beyond the parties' actual positions?
- **Expectation.** @tbl-predictions, row 3: the excess over actual spread discriminates.
- **Exhibit.** $\Delta$ in perceived spread and in its excess over a benchmark; out-party vs. in-party placements.
- **Limits.** Sophistication; scale use; exploratory (@sec-limitations).
:::

## Perceived Party Sorting {#sec-res-perceived-sorting}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** Do explicit partisans perceive the parties' LR and EU positions as more aligned than deniers of the same party, and beyond the actual alignment?
- **Expectation.** @tbl-predictions, row 4: the excess over actual alignment discriminates.
- **Exhibit.** $\Delta$ in perceived alignment and in its excess.
- **Limits.** Few placed parties per respondent; sophistication (@sec-limitations).
:::

## Vertical Attitudinal Affective Polarization {#sec-res-vertical}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** Is the gap between ratings of one's own party and the out-parties larger for explicit partisans than for deniers of the same party, does it persist at equal policy distance, and is it located in in-party or out-party ratings?
  Do mismatched partisans rate their attachment party or their vote party higher?
- **Expectation.** @tbl-predictions, row 5.
- **Exhibit.** $\Delta$ unadjusted and at equal distance to the rated party; in-party and out-party components; the within-person rating of the attachment party against the vote party; EES 2024 ratings of party supporters as the horizontal attitudinal complement.
- **Limits.** Selection through the vote; distance-adjusted estimates are controlled direct effects; PTV is not a pure measure of affect (@sec-limitations).
:::

## Horizontal Behavioral Affective Polarization {#sec-res-behavioral}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** Is the effect of the partner's party label larger for explicit partisans than for deniers, and is the difference located in favoritism or in derogation?
  Is the behavioral gap comparable to the attitudinal gap in the same respondents?
- **Expectation.** @tbl-predictions, row 6.
- **Exhibit.** $AP_t$ by type, split into favoritism and derogation; the gradient in the partner party's distance; behavioral against attitudinal $\Delta$ in standard-deviation units.
- **Limits.** $\Delta$ is not randomized; one year; few co-partisan partners for deniers (@sec-limitations).
:::

## The Profile {#sec-res-profile}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** RQ2: which reading does the pattern of $\Delta$ across facets fit?
- **Exhibit.** $\Delta$ for each facet in standard-deviation units, in ladder order, with leaners and mismatched partisans, set against the patterns the three readings predict (@sec-ladder).
- **Reading.** A flat profile at zero favors the functional reading, a falling profile the evaluative reading, a rising profile the identity reading.
  A mixed profile indicates which kind of attachment European partisanship is on which facet.
:::

# Where Attachment Matters {#sec-where}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** RQ3: how does $\Delta$ vary across countries and parties?
- **Exhibit.** $\Delta$ by country for the facets with the best coverage; $\Delta$ for cleavage parties, for parties of the new cultural cleavage and by the polarization of the party system.
- **Reading.** Against the expectations in @sec-context-expectations; descriptive, not a test of context effects.
- **Limits.** 25 countries; noisy measures of context (@sec-limitations).
:::

# Composition and Polarization within Types {#sec-decomposition}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned analysis"}
- **Question.** RQ4: how much of the change in polarization over time, and of the differences between countries, reflects the mix of partisan types, and how much reflects polarization within types?
- **Exhibit.** The decomposition by country and by the trajectory identified in @sec-composition; a counterfactual partisan-only index that shows how such a measure would have ranked countries and trends.
- **Reading.** Against the expectations in @sec-change-expectations.
- **Limits.** Age, period and cohort are not separated; few elections per country; the dynamics are not read causally (@sec-limitations).
:::

# Limitations and Open Issues {#sec-limitations}

This section collects the limitations of the design and the issues that remain open.
It serves both as the limitations section of the paper and as a record of what must not be forgotten as the analyses proceed.

## Identification {#sec-lim-identification}

The within-party contrast does not hold fixed individual characteristics that shape both attachment and polarization, such as age and socialization, parental partisanship, political interest and ideological intensity.
A causal reading of $\Delta$ would require that attachment is as good as random given party, country and characteristics that precede it; that the vote does not select respondents on the outcome; and that a type means the same across wordings.
None of these is guaranteed.

- **Selection through the vote.** Deniers may vote for their party partly because they dislike the alternatives.
  This plausibly pulls the AP gap toward zero.
  The mismatched group is itself selected on voting against its attachment.
- **Reverse causation for ideology.** Citizens with extreme or coherent views may attach because a party fits them.
  Selection on proximity makes deniers look less extreme at centrist parties and more extreme at parties on the flanks; the gap by party position tests this.
- **Sophistication for perception.** Attachment goes with political sophistication, which may make perceptions of the parties more accurate rather than more biased.
  Benchmarks and corrections for scale use narrow this confound but do not remove it.
- **Controlled direct effects.** Holding policy distance fixed in the AP analyses yields a controlled direct effect, because distance is partly a consequence of attachment.
- **The games.** The label effect is causal for each type, but $\Delta$ is a difference in a causal effect by a moderator that is not randomized, and it inherits every confounding problem of the types.
  The party label also carries inferred policy.
- **Uncertainty.** The posterior reflects sampling and the assumptions of pooling.
  It does not reflect selection or the composition of a group.
  Where a type is rare in a country, this shows as wider uncertainty.
- **Triangulation.** A pattern that is robust across sources can still be robustly biased by confounding that all sources share.

## Measurement {#sec-lim-measurement}

- **Wording.** Items ask about closeness, which may differ from identification [@elliott2024like].
  The ESS item asks whether a party is closer than all others and so already takes in some leaners.
  Wording differs by source and, in the EES, by wave.
- **Leaners.** The leaner probe exists only in the CSES and the EES 2009.
  Elsewhere, leaners are counted among deniers if they voted and among non-partisans if they did not, so a denier in the ESS or EU25 is not the same category as a probed denier in the CSES.
  A leaner who voted for another party is kept apart from the mismatched type and reported only where cells allow.
- **Translations in EU25.** The Italian item asks about a relative attachment, and the Danish and Greek items ask about sharing a party's views.
- **Multiple attachments.** Single-party items cannot record attachments to more than one party [@block2026partisan].
- **The vote.** Recalled votes carry error.
  In EU25, the wave-1 vote item is the intended vote at the 2019 European Parliament election.
- **Question order.** In most surveys the vote is asked before the attachment item; CSES Module 3 is the exception.
- **Outcomes.** PTV ratings mix affect with assessments of a party's viability and are treated as a separate operationalization.
  The EU attribute in the games is an identity cue, not a policy position, and so offers no randomized test of party against policy.

## Party Matching and Types {#sec-lim-matching}

- Whether the attachment party is the party voted for is decided by one rule across all sources, which counts identical parties, aliases, alliances and lineage as the same party.
  Counting lineage as the same party is a deliberate choice; the route of every match is recorded, so analyses can exclude it.
- Alliances and successor parties need an audit before the mismatched type is interpreted.
- The mismatched group mixes strategic and coalition voting, multiple attachments, recall error and matching artifacts.
  Mismatches within an ideological bloc are separated from mismatches across blocs before interpretation.
- Hand decisions in the Party Facts coding are documented in the preparation notebooks and must be reviewed for the parties that drive the estimates.

## Data and Coverage {#sec-lim-coverage}

- Coverage of the EU dimension is thinner than coverage of LR.
  The CSES has no EU items, no ratings of party supporters and no games.
- The EES 2024 ratings of party supporters come from different respondents and a different year than the games, so the comparison of horizontal attitudinal with horizontal behavioral AP is descriptive.
- In the EU25 games, partners' parties were drawn from the attachment answer.
  Attached respondents meet a co-partisan in about half the rounds, deniers only by chance, so the denier cells with co-partisan partners are thin.
  In Latvia, the draw for respondents without an attachment copied their answer that they feel close to no party.
  The games cover one election year.
- Few elections per country make country-specific trends rely on the prior.
- A coverage table of item × study × round × country, checked against the codebooks, is the first deliverable and decides which facets enter the comparative and dynamic analyses.

## Comparative and Dynamic Inference {#sec-lim-dynamic}

- With 25 countries and noisy measures of context, variation across countries is described rather than explained.
- Age, period and cohort are not separated.
  Over-time patterns are interpreted with this in mind and are not read causally.
- Trends may reflect switching between studies and wordings rather than change in electorates; robustness to dropping single studies is checked.

## Open Design Decisions {#sec-lim-open}

- The centre against which extremity is measured: the scale midpoint, the country mean or the median.
  Alternatives will be reported.
- The measure of sorting: a flexible association measured within countries, with magnitudes pooled, never raw correlations.
- The likelihood for each facet, chosen by predictive checks.
- How to display differences in wording across surveys, following @boxell2024cross.

## Literature Still to Be Consulted {#sec-lim-literature}

- The classic texts cited in @sec-intro and @sec-concepts for standard claims [@campbell1960american; @budge1976party; @shively1979development; @fiorina1981retrospective; @green2004partisan] must be checked against the texts before submission.
- European evidence on perceived polarization by partisan type has not yet been located.

## Questions for the Workshop {#sec-lim-workshop}

1. Is the opening on the population of inference convincing as a motivation, or does it read as a measurement note?
2. Are the functional, evaluative and identity readings the right map, and is the in-group/out-group split of the identity reading useful?
3. Is the ladder of facets an intuitive order for presenting expectations and results?
4. Should the games, or the composition analysis, be a separate paper?

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

::: {.callout-note title="Planned"}
- One paragraph per RQ: the partisan composition of European electorates; what partisanship is in Europe, as the profile reads it; where it matters; and whose polarization is measured when partisan-only measures are used.
- Recommendations for measurement: the population of inference, the definition of the in-party, and closeness versus identity items.
- The American party-versus-policy debate revisited: what holding the party's policy signal fixed allows, and what it does not.
- What kind of attachment European partisanship is, and whether it is the kind that serves democracy [@elliott2024like; @bankert2023politics].
:::

Return to the opening question: whose polarization is measured, and what partisanship adds to it.
:::


# Empirical Analysis

## RQ1: Partisanship in Europe in the 21st Century

- **Levels.** How are electorates split into the types (explicit, denier, leaner, mismatched, attached non-voter, non-partisan), pooled and by country? (Fig. 1, pooled panel)
- **Dealignment.** Has the share reporting an attachment fallen since 2002, and where? If so, by detachment (explicit → denier: still voting, no tie) or by disengagement (→ non-partisan: neither)? (Fig. 1, 25 country panels, ESS lines)
- **Realignment.** Does attachment follow the vote to new-cleavage families (green, radical right)? Their share among partisans against their share among voters, i.e. conversion P(attached | voted for family). (Fig. 2)
- **Measurement.** How much of the level differences between countries and sources is the item wording (ESS "closer than others" vs. EES/CSES "close to"; probed leaners in the CSES)? (EES/CSES points beside the ESS lines; leaner share of CSES deniers)
- **Who the deniers are.** Do deniers resemble explicit partisans or non-partisans on pre-treatment traits (age, education, interest)? Bridge to RQ2 (bracketing diagnostic) and RQ4 (concentration vs. alienation).
- **Support for RQ2.** In which party × country cells do explicit partisans and deniers both occur in usable numbers, and how large and how cross-bloc is the mismatched group?

## RQ2: Partisanship and Polarization in Europe

- how do partisan types differ with respect to polarization?
- facets of polarization: ideological (LR & EU), sorting (LR & EU), perceived party (LR & EU), perceived sorting (LR & EU), affective polarization (attitudinal vertical & horizontal behavioral, latter only 2019, both with focus on ingroup and outgroup)
- pooled type contrasts on each outcome

## RQ3: Cross-national patterns and over time trends 

- do and if so how do the associations between partisan types and polarization measures differ between countries?
- how do they develop over time?
- within country over time?

## RQ4: Are observed changes in polarization driven by changing partisan compositions or changing polarization within partisan types?

- are over time trends attributable to composition changes or reflect actual increases of polarization? What is the relative share of each (x% of polarization is attributable to composition change (e.g. realignment), y% is due to partisans / people themself becoming more polarized)
